plain: Proposition 133 would make life in prison without parole the required sentence for child sex trafficking. It would also add buying sex with a minor to what counts as child sex trafficking.

short_version.text: Proposition 133 would make child sex trafficking punishable only by life without parole, instead of 8 to 48 years, and remove judges' discretion. Few cases reach court each year; about a third of trafficking cases end in a trafficking conviction, and most of the rest in a conviction on another charge. State costs would begin in about 14 years.

agree_means: Yes makes life without parole mandatory for anyone convicted of child sex trafficking, buyers and sellers alike, and takes away the judge's choice of sentence.
disagree_means: No keeps the current sentence of 8 to 48 years in prison plus a mandatory parole period, set by a judge within that range.

example.text: Colorado courts handled 46 cases of minor sex trafficking in 2023. Under Proposition 133, a conviction on that charge would mean life without parole; today a judge picks a term between 8 and 48 years.

stakes.text: Deterrence research: the National Institute of Justice says the certainty of being caught deters crime far more than the severity of punishment. Raising severity does little.

sources.title: Five Things About Deterrence (National Institute of Justice)
sources.quote: The certainty of being caught is a vastly more powerful deterrent than the punishment.

sources.title: Five Things About Deterrence (National Institute of Justice)
sources.quote: Increasing the severity of punishment does little to deter crime.

stakes.text: The Legislature considered the same idea in HB26-1082, and a House committee killed it on Feb 10, 2026. Research on federal mandatory minimums found prosecutors often use their discretion to avoid overly severe results, so outcomes varied.

sources.quote: The bill modifies the crime of human trafficking of a minor for sexual servitude and makes it a class 1 felony.

case_for.text: Supporters, including Protect Kids Colorado, say child sex trafficking is among the most serious crimes. They say people who buy or sell children for sex should spend their lives in prison, and that tougher penalties could deter traffickers.

sources.title: Proposition 133: Penalties for human trafficking of minors (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: Supporters, including Protect Kids Colorado, argue that child sex trafficking is among the most serious crimes and that those who buy or sell children for sex should spend the rest of their lives in prison.

case_for.text: The Blue Book's argument for the measure adds that the punishment is clear and definite and ensures offenders cannot hurt more children.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: The punishment outlined in the measure is clear, definite, and ensures that offenders cannot hurt more children.

case_against.text: Opponents, including the Colorado Coalition Against Sexual Assault, say judges should keep the power to weigh each case's circumstances.

sources.title: Proposition 133: Penalties for human trafficking of minors (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: Opponents, including the Colorado Coalition Against Sexual Assault, argue that sentencing decisions should remain in judges’ hands, who can consider the specific circumstances of each case.

case_against.text: Opponents say fear of a life sentence could make victims less likely to report or cooperate with police.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: Due to the fear of a life sentence, victims may be less likely to report these crimes or cooperate with police.

unknowns.text: How prosecutors would charge and plea cases under a mandatory life term is unknown. State data show many trafficking-charged cases already end in convictions on other charges.

research_notes: Claude in Chrome was not connected; no page for this file needed the browser. The court-case counts (21, 46, 21 minor sex trafficking cases; 25, 28, 13 concluded cases of all trafficking types with 4, 12, 6 trafficking convictions) were read from bar charts (Figures 20 and 28) on PDF pages 22 and 29 (report pages 38 and 45) of the Colorado Human Trafficking Council's 2025 report; the charts are images, so the quotes only confirm the figure text, not the numbers. A reviewer should open those two pages. 'Convicted Other' in Figure 28 is read as conviction on another charge, per the report's next sentence about ancillary charges. Those counts are filings in the state court system for all trafficking types (adult, labor, minor) and may not equal prosecutions per year of the specific offense this measure changes; I found no count limited to the offense under C.R.S. 18-3-504. The U.S. Sentencing Commission finding is about federal mandatory minimums in 2011, not Colorado or sex offenses. The NIJ brief is general deterrence research. The HB26-1082 committee summary says 'Postponed Indefinitely' (Feb 10, 2026); I did not read the written testimony. I found no district attorney position on Prop 133 and no source on plea bargaining under mandatory life terms in Colorado. Web search budget ran out mid-session. Editor, 2026-10-16: the minor sex-trafficking counts (21, 46, 21) are quoted from the data row under Figure 20; the disposition counts (4, 12, 6 trafficking convictions; 19, 13, 6 convicted on other charges; 2, 3, 1 dismissed) were read from the Figure 28 chart image on page 45 of the section PDF, which covers all trafficking cases, not only minors.
